intro: Breda's oldest trees survived by getting in the way of a building, not by being protected on purpose. A trio of mulberries stopped a 1995 library architect from building where he first planned to, a wingnut from the Caucasus outgrew the fashion that planted it, and a giant sequoia keeps growing beside a street named for the village it is not quite in. None of it is planned heritage. All of it is free to see, in a city better known for its Golden Triangle nightlife than for what is quietly growing behind it.
meta_description: Breda's oldest trees are three 1780s mulberries a library was built around. Ten verified trees, real stories, how to reach each one.
question_answer: Breda's oldest trees are three black mulberries in the inner courtyard of De Nieuwe Veste on Molenstraat, planted around 1780 in the garden of the manor house Huize Ocrum, roughly 245 years old. Architect Herman Hertzberger built the current library and cultural centre around them in 1995 rather than remove them.
question_meta: Three 1780s mulberry trees, built around by a 1995 library, are Breda's oldest. Where to find them, and the city's other nine verified ancient trees.
question_context: The mulberries' age comes from the property's own recorded history rather than a ring count: Huize Ocrum's garden is documented as the planting site around 1780, under its then-owner Gerrit Willem Motman, steward of the princely domains, and the trees survived as the surrounding estate was built up and eventually demolished around them over the following two centuries. When Herman Hertzberger designed the current De Nieuwe Veste library and cultural centre in the mid-1990s, the three trees were already old enough that removing them was never seriously considered. Instead the building folds around the courtyard they stand in, their canopy shaping the layout of the structure above rather than the other way round, an unusually literal case of architecture following an existing tree rather than clearing space for a new one. They are not the tallest or thickest trees in Breda; the courtyard is small and the trees have grown accordingly. Their claim to being the city's oldest rests on the documented planting date alone, which none of Breda's other candidate trees can currently match with the same specificity.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Breda?
faq.a: Three black mulberries in the courtyard of De Nieuwe Veste on Molenstraat, planted around 1780 in what was then the garden of Huize Ocrum, roughly 245 years old.

faq.q: Are Breda's ancient trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, all ten are in public parks or a public library courtyard with free access during opening hours.

faq.q: Why does a library in Breda have trees growing inside its courtyard?
faq.a: The mulberries at De Nieuwe Veste predate the current 1995 building by over two centuries. Architect Herman Hertzberger designed the library and cultural centre around them rather than remove them.

faq.q: What is the Caucasian wingnut in Valkenberg park?
faq.a: A Pterocarya fraxinifolia planted around 1830, roughly 195 years old, with a trunk nearly 6 metres around, growing in Breda's central park beside Breda Castle and the Grote Kerk.

trees.name: The Mulberries of Nieuwe Veste
trees.story: A library was built around these trees rather than the other way round. Three black mulberries have grown in this small courtyard since around 1780, when it was still the garden of Huize Ocrum, a manor house owned at the time by Gerrit Willem Motman, steward of the Dutch princely domains. The house came down over the following two centuries as the site changed hands and purpose, but the mulberries stayed, and when architect Herman Hertzberger designed De Nieuwe Veste, Breda's combined library, music school and cultural centre, in the mid-1990s, he folded the new building's plan around the courtyard rather than clear it. The trees now shape the layout of a public building constructed more than two hundred years after they were planted, an unusually literal case of architecture yielding to something already there. At roughly 245 years old they are, as far as any documented planting date in Breda goes, the city's oldest living trees, though the courtyard they stand in is modest and the trees themselves are not large by monumental-tree standards elsewhere in the country. Free to visit during the library's opening hours, they are also one of the few entries on this list a visitor can reach without ever stepping outside.
trees.access: Free, public library and cultural centre, open during opening hours
trees.transport: Central Breda, Molenstraat; 10 minute walk from Breda railway station

best_time.label: August into September, when the mulberries ripen

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the count, three black mulberries in one small courtyard, and by the building folded around them rather than through them. They stand inside De Nieuwe Veste on the Molenstraat, reached without going outside.

trees.name: The Trumpet Tree of Wilhelminapark
trees.story: This catalpa grew sideways instead of up, and Breda decided to help it keep doing so. It leans out over the pond in Wilhelminapark, a park laid out in 1894 by landscape architect Leonard A. Springer, far enough over the water that the municipality now props its lowest limbs on columns rather than let them snap or drag. Local tradition credits Queen Wilhelmina herself, the park's namesake, with intervening at some point to see the tree preserved rather than felled for convenience, though the story's exact origin is harder to pin down than the tree's current, very visible lean. Catalpas are not native to the Netherlands, brought from the southeastern United States as an ornamental species prized for its huge heart-shaped leaves and its white, purple-throated flower spikes in midsummer, and this one has had well over a century in Dutch soil to develop the sprawling, horizontal habit the species is capable of when nothing stops it. No exact planting record survives, so its age is inferred from the park's own founding date rather than documented outright. Wilhelminapark itself has lost several of its other historic trees in recent years to disease and storm damage, which makes this one's continued, actively supported survival more notable rather than less.
trees.transport: Zandberg neighbourhood, Breda; 15 minute walk from Breda railway station

best_time.label: July, when the catalpa's white flower spikes open

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lean and the props: it grows sideways out over the pond, its lowest limbs held up on columns by the city. It stands at the water in Wilhelminapark, under big heart-shaped leaves.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Valkenberg
trees.story: A tree from the mountains between the Black and Caspian Seas has been growing in Breda's oldest park for close to two centuries. This Caucasian wingnut, planted around 1830 in Valkenberg beside Breda Castle and the Grote Kerk, was measured in September 2020 at 5.82 metres around, a size that reflects how fast and wide the species spreads once established rather than any particular rarity of specimen. Wingnuts were a genuine curiosity in 19th-century Dutch parks, planted by landscape designers testing what exotic species could handle the local climate, and this one has clearly handled it: its suckering roots have likely spread new stems around the original trunk over the decades, the species' usual habit when left alone in open ground. Valkenberg itself predates the tree by centuries, laid out on the grounds beside Breda Castle, once the seat of the House of Nassau and now a military academy, with the Grote Kerk's tower visible over the park's mature tree canopy. The wingnut is one of several genuinely old trees in the park, including planes and horse chestnuts pushing a century themselves, but its size and unusual leaf, long pinnate fronds rather than a single broad leaf, make it the one visitors actually stop under.
trees.transport: Central Breda, beside Breda Castle; 10 minute walk from Breda railway station

best_time.label: July to September: long green catkins of winged nutlets hang from every branch

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaf, long pinnate fronds rather than one broad blade, and by the trunk, measured at 5.82 metres round in September 2020. It stands in Valkenberg among the park's planes and horse chestnuts.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of Laurenspark
trees.story: Despite its name, Ulvenhoutselaan runs inside Breda, not the separate village of Ulvenhout the street is named after, and this giant sequoia stands well within city limits along it, in the Ginneken district in the south of town. Planted in 1885, measured at 25 metres tall and 5.70 metres around, it belongs to the wave of Californian conifers that spread through Dutch estates and parks in the second half of the 19th century, after the species was first introduced to Europe in the 1850s and became, briefly, a fashionable statement for anyone with land to plant on. At 140 years old it has had time to become a genuinely large tree by Dutch standards without coming close to challenging its own species' natural lifespan, which can run past two thousand years in California's Sierra Nevada. Ginneken itself was a separate village until it merged into Breda in the 20th century, which makes the sequoia's setting a small irony of its own: a street named for a village that is not this tree's home, in a neighbourhood that used to be a different one. Free to see, in a quiet residential park rather than a tourist destination, it rewards anyone who already knows where to look.
trees.transport: Ginneken, Breda; bus from Breda railway station or a 25 minute walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the size, twenty-five metres tall and 5.70 metres round, a giant sequoia planted in 1885. It stands in Laurenspark on the Ulvenhoutselaan, in the Ginneken district south of the centre.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Wilhelminapark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 126 to 136 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900

location.address: Wilhelminapark, west side of the pond, Breda

trees.story:
The lowest branches of this beech touch the ground and can root back into it, so what looks like one tree is quietly capable of becoming a ring of them.

That habit is what a weeping beech does when nobody stops it. The straight trunk throws its branches out and down instead of up, and where a branch tip lies against damp soil for long enough it can strike its own roots, a trick foresters call layering. Duck under the canopy at Wilhelminapark's western pond edge and you are standing inside a room the tree built for itself, walled by drooping branches on every side and lit green through the leaves.

The register puts its planting in the 1890s, which makes it a First World War contemporary standing quietly in a park that also holds a Polish war memorial and a captured German tank nearby. Nobody has recorded its age more precisely than the decade it was planted, and a trunk this size does not need a precise number to be worth ducking into.

Free, public park, open daily.

Come in winter if you want to see the architecture. Bare, the cascading branch structure of a weeping beech reads more dramatic than in full leaf, when the canopy is one solid green mass instead of a hundred draped ribs.
trees.transport: Zandberg neighbourhood, Breda; 15 minute walk from Breda railway station.
trees.how_to_recognise: Branches that arch down and touch the soil on every side, forming a green tent you can walk into, on the pond's west edge.

best_time.label: winter, when the bare branches show the tent-like cascade

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of Vijverstraat
trees.age_estimate: roughly 126 to 136 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900
trees.story:
This wingnut carries its seeds in chains that can run half a metre long, dozens of winged nuts strung like beads down a single stalk.

Pterocarya fraxinifolia is a Caucasian native in the same family as the walnut, and it shows: crush a leaf and the smell is unmistakably a walnut cousin's. It throws up multiple trunks from the base rather than one clean stem, which is normal for the species rather than damage, and it grows fast enough that a specimen planted in the late nineteenth century can already dwarf a chestnut planted the same decade.

Breda has two of these registered within a kilometre of each other, this one on the Vijverstraat corner of Wilhelminapark, the other across town in Valkenberg beside the castle grounds. This is the more sheltered of the pair, tucked among the park's older plantings rather than standing in the open.

The register bands its planting to 1890 to 1900, putting it past its first century. No girth has been recorded.

Free, public park, open daily.

Look for the seed chains from midsummer into autumn. Nothing else in a Dutch park hangs quite like this.
trees.transport: Zandberg neighbourhood, Breda; 15 minute walk from Breda railway station.
trees.how_to_recognise: The more sheltered of Breda's two registered wingnuts, multi-stemmed from the base, on the Vijverstraat corner of the park.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of the Stone Bench
trees.age_estimate: roughly 156 to 166 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870

location.address: Wilhelminapark, middle of the southern section near the stone bench, Breda

trees.story:
Turn one of this lime's leaves over and the underside is a soft, felted silver, which is where the species gets its name and why the whole crown seems to flicker when wind moves through it.

Tilia tomentosa is planted across Dutch parks for exactly that effect: from a distance a silver lime in a breeze looks like it is catching light no other tree nearby is catching. This one stands in the middle of Wilhelminapark's southern section, near a stone bench that has clearly been positioned to sit under it rather than merely beside it.

The register dates its planting to the 1860s, making it the oldest of several silver limes recorded in this park and one of the older trees in central Breda still standing where it was planted. It flowers later than most limes, into July, and the scent from a tree this size carries well past the bench.

Free, public park, open daily.

Come in July for the flowering. The rest of the year it is a fine shade tree; for two or three weeks in high summer it is the most fragrant spot in the park.
trees.transport: Zandberg neighbourhood, Breda; 15 minute walk from Breda railway station.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oldest of the park's several silver limes, standing over a stone bench positioned to sit beneath it.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers late and the scent fills this end of the park

trees.name: The Beech of Paul Withausenweg
trees.age_estimate: roughly 126 to 136 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900

location.address: Wilhelminapark, middle section along Paul Withausenweg, Breda

trees.story:
This is the plain, green-leaved beech among a park that otherwise favours its copper and weeping cousins, which makes it the least conspicuous registered tree in Wilhelminapark and one of the largest.

Fagus sylvatica is the wild-type European beech, the species every ornamental copper and weeping form has been bred from, and left to grow straight and green it does the thing beeches do best: a dense, smooth-barked trunk holding up a crown so complete that almost nothing grows in the deep shade beneath it. In the park's middle section, along the Paul Withausenweg, it stands among younger, more colourful plantings without competing for attention.

The register bands its planting to 1890 to 1900, putting it just past its first century and a quarter. No girth has been recorded.

Free, public park, open daily.

There is no single dramatic month for a green beech the way there is for its copper relatives elsewhere in this park. Autumn brings a plain gold rather than the copper's colour, but the trunk and the shade it throws are worth the visit at any time of year.
trees.transport: Zandberg neighbourhood, Breda; 15 minute walk from Breda railway station.
trees.how_to_recognise: The plain green-leaved beech among the park's copper and weeping forms, along the Paul Withausenweg.

trees.name: The Tallest Oak of Valkenberg
trees.age_estimate: roughly 136 to 146 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Valkenberg park, near the J.F. Kennedylaan, Breda

trees.story:
The register itself calls this the tallest pedunculate oak in Valkenberg, which is a real claim rather than a guess, since somebody with the right instrument had to measure every registered oak in the park to say so.

Quercus robur is the oak native to this part of Europe, the one an acorn falling in October will grow into if left alone, and Valkenberg has several registered specimens. This one has simply outgrown its neighbours, reaching well above the park's tree line near the J.F. Kennedylaan side of the grounds.

The register bands its planting to 1880 to 1890, so it has had roughly a century and a half to win that height. No further age detail and no girth are recorded.

Free, public park, open daily. Valkenberg is Breda's central city park, beside the castle grounds.

There is no single dramatic month for an oak like this. It is worth finding for the same reason it was measured: to stand under the tallest one and see, by comparison, how much smaller the rest of the park's oaks actually are.
trees.transport: Central Breda, beside Breda Castle; 10 minute walk from Breda railway station.
trees.how_to_recognise: The register's own tallest pedunculate oak in the park, standing above the surrounding tree line near the J.F. Kennedylaan.

trees.name: The Plane of Valkenberg's Edge
trees.age_estimate: roughly 136 to 146 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Willemstraat / John F. Kennedylaan, edge of Valkenberg park, Breda

trees.story:
This plane's bark comes away in patches the size of a hand, which is not disease. London planes shed their bark in irregular plates because the trunk cannot expand fast enough to keep an unbroken skin, and the patchwork of grey, green and cream underneath is the tree's normal, healthy state.

It stands on the western rim of Valkenberg, at the corner where the park gives way to the Willemstraat and the John F. Kennedylaan, which is why it registers to a slightly different address than the trees deeper in the park despite being part of the same grounds.

The register bands its planting to the 1880s, and London planes of that age are common street and park trees across the Netherlands precisely because they tolerate compacted soil and traffic pollution better than almost anything else that gets this large. That toughness, not rarity, is the reason to notice it: a tree planted for a hard job that has quietly outlived every reason it was chosen for.

Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: Central Breda, beside Breda Castle; 10 minute walk from Breda railway station.
trees.how_to_recognise: The plane standing at the park's western edge, where Valkenberg gives way to the Willemstraat corner.
